n: Wadi Al Khlata (Al Khlata Formation type section)
s: Type section of Oman’s ice-age rocks · glacial deposits and striated pavements of the Haushi–Huqf uplift
dr: Al Khlata Formation, Haushi Group: late Moscovian–Asselian (about 311–294 Ma)
el: About 100 m thick at the type section; over 800 m in the subsurface
se: In the Huqf desert, rocks left by glaciers about 300 million years ago still show boulders and pavements scratched by moving ice
sa: في صحراء الحقف ما زالت صخور خلّفتها الأنهار الجليدية قبل نحو 300 مليون عام تحمل جلاميد وأرضيات صخرية خدشها الجليد في أثناء زحفه
desc: Wadi Al Khlata, on the Haushi–Huqf uplift of central Oman, is the type section of the Al Khlata Formation, the glacially influenced base of the Haushi Group, about 100 m thick here. The formation spans the late Moscovian to Asselian (about 311–294 Ma) and consists of diamictites, conglomerates, gravels, pebbly sandstones, siltstones and shales, including laminated shales with dropstones and faceted, striated boulders up to a metre across. Its glacial origin is established by striated pavements cut into the Precambrian Khufai Formation on the western flank of the uplift, whose crag-and-tail features show ice moving towards the north-east. In the subsurface the formation varies from about 100 m to more than 800 m thick and forms hydrocarbon reservoirs.
sig: The reference outcrop for the Late Palaeozoic glaciation of Arabia, when the region lay in southern Gondwana, and a key analogue for Oman’s Al Khlata oil and gas reservoirs.
ex: Stephenson et al. (2013); Middle East Geological Lexicon
refs: Stephenson, M.H., Jan, I.U. & Al-Mashaikie, S.Z.A.K. (2013). Palynology and correlation of Carboniferous–Permian glacigene rocks in Oman, Yemen and Pakistan. Gondwana Research 24(1), 203–211. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gr.2012.06.005
Middle East Geological Lexicon. Al Khlata Formation (Oman). https://mideastlex.geolex.org/formations/Al%20Khlata%20Fm
conf: Coordinates are the published type-section point 19°46′43″N, 57°25′46″E (Stephenson et al. 2013), second precision; timeline uses the lexicon’s 311.09–293.52 Ma range; Arabic الخلطة is a careful transliteration. About 30 km from Duqm Rock Garden and 38 km from Wadi Shuram

s: Southernmost surface salt dome of central Oman · carries rare fragments of buried basement
dr: Andesite clast dated about 545 Ma (U–Pb zircon); sandstone clast deposited after about 734 Ma
te: A salt elevator from deep below
se: Rising salt at Qarn Sahmah has carried up pieces of volcanic rock from kilometres underground that no one could otherwise reach
sa: رفع الملح الصاعد في قرن سهمة قطعًا من صخور بركانية من أعماق تبلغ كيلومترات، يستحيل الوصول إليها بغير ذلك
desc: Qarn Sahmah is the southernmost of the surface-piercing salt domes of interior central Oman, whose Ara salt carries limestone blocks of the Ara Group up to several hundred metres across. Of the central Oman domes visited by Thomas et al. (2015), only Qarn Sahmah also contains volcanic and sedimentary clasts, concentrated in a small central area; the northern group of five domes holds only Ara Formation clasts. A porphyritic andesite from the dome gave a U–Pb zircon crystallisation age of about 545 Ma, and a red sandstone a maximum depositional age of about 734 Ma. The volcanic samples have ocean-island-basalt-like chemistry with positive Nb–Ta anomalies.
sig: One of very few windows into the hidden Neoproterozoic basement of eastern Arabia, brought to the surface by salt from great depth.
refs: Thomas, R.J., Ellison, R.A., Goodenough, K.M., Roberts, N.M.W. & Allen, P.A. (2015). Salt domes of the UAE and Oman: probing eastern Arabia. Precambrian Research 256, 1–16. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.precamres.2014.10.011
conf: Coordinates converted from the published sample location of andesite RTOM_9 (457472 E, 2278854 N; Thomas et al. 2015, Table 3), read as UTM zone 40N WGS84 because the paper states no datum or zone; precision ≈ a few hundred metres. Governorate assigned from the coordinate. Arabic قرن سهمة is a careful transliteration. Timeline start is the andesite age; the dome itself is still active

na: مقاطع تكوين الخف عند قبة حوشي
s: Middle Permian sea-floor fossils of the Huqf · the Khuff sea’s edge in central Oman
el: Khuff Formation up to 30–40 m thick
te: Shells of a vanished Permian sea
se: On the flank of the Haushi uplift, marls and limestones are packed with brachiopods and tiny conodonts from a sea that flooded Oman about 265 million years ago
sa: على جانب قبة حوشي تزخر طبقات المارل والحجر الجيري بالعضديات وأحافير الكونودونت الدقيقة من بحر غمر عُمان قبل نحو 265 مليون عام
desc: Five sections along the north-western flank of the Haushi uplift in the Huqf area expose the Khuff Formation, a succession of marine marls and bioclastic limestones up to 30–40 m thick, divided into four members and deposited on an outer shelf. It overlies fluvial rocks of the Gharif Formation and is cut by an angular unconformity beneath the continental Minjur Formation. The beds yield brachiopods (mainly productids, with a mixed fauna dominated by Tethyan genera), conodonts including Hindeodus excavatus and Merrillina praedivergens, foraminifera, bivalves, gastropods, ostracods and cephalopods. Angiolini et al. (1998) assigned the formation here a provisional Wordian (Guadalupian, Middle Permian) age.
sig: Fixes the age of the Khuff marine transgression in south-eastern Oman with fossils, at the edge of the Permian Tethys sea.
refs: Angiolini, L., Nicora, A., Bucher, H., Vachard, D., Pillevuit, A., Platel, J.-P., Roger, J., Baud, A., Broutin, J., Al Hashmi, H. & Marcoux, J. (1998). Evidence of a Guadalupian age for the Khuff Formation of southeastern Oman: preliminary report. Rivista Italiana di Paleontologia e Stratigrafia 104(3), 329–340. https://riviste.unimi.it/index.php/RIPS/article/view/5337
conf: Coordinates are the western end of the published span 21°00′37″N 57°39′35″E to 21°02′06″N 57°41′23″E (Angiolini et al. 1998; text partly garbled by OCR, first point read as given), second precision. Timeline uses the ICS 2023 Wordian bounds (266.9–264.28 Ma), not a date from the paper. Arabic الخف and حوشي are the usual transliterations; governorate assigned from the coordinate near the Al Wusta boundary

s: Dried-up Late Pleistocene lake in the Omani interior · a possible stepping stone for early humans
el: Lake and river deposits from a humid phase 132,000–104,000 years ago
te: A lake in the middle of the desert
se: Near Saiwan, old lake mud in today’s desert shows that rain once filled a lake here, perhaps helping early humans cross Arabia
sa: قرب سيوان تكشف رواسب بحيرة قديمة وسط الصحراء أن الأمطار ملأت هنا بحيرة يومًا، ولعلها أعانت البشر الأوائل على عبور جزيرة العرب
desc: Near Saiwan in central Oman, relict lake sediments first noted in an earlier reconnaissance were studied by Rosenberg as part of a doctoral project on humid phases recorded in Arabian lake deposits. The fluvial and lacustrine deposits record a short humid period sometime between 132,000 and 104,000 years ago. The area is noted for its rich archaeological evidence, and Rosenberg et al. (2012) proposed the palaeolake as a potential key area for the dispersal of anatomically modern humans out of Africa.
sig: Evidence that the now hyper-arid interior of Oman held a lake between 132,000 and 104,000 years ago, a possible route for modern humans spreading out of Africa.
refs: Rosenberg, T.M., Preusser, F., Blechschmidt, I., Fleitmann, D., Jagher, R. & Matter, A. (2012). Late Pleistocene palaeolake in the interior of Oman: a potential key area for the dispersal of anatomically modern humans out-of-Africa? Journal of Quaternary Science 27(1), 13–16. https://doi.org/10.1002/jqs.1560
Rosenberg, T.M. (2011). Palaeoclimate history of the Arabian Peninsula: humid phases recorded in lake deposits. PhD thesis, University of Bern. https://occrdata.unibe.ch/students/theses/phd/72.pdf
conf: Coordinates are the Oman sample site 20°58′N, 57°22′E given in Rosenberg (2011, ch. 2), minute precision (≈1–2 km); the thesis’s only Oman study area is the palaeolake near Saiwan, but the text does not name the site at that point. Lake size and individual luminescence ages were not available. Arabic سيوان is a careful transliteration; governorate assigned from the coordinate

n: Mudhmar East Iron Age ritual site
na: موقع مضمار الشرقي من العصر الحديدي
s: Iron Age ritual buildings near Adam · bronze weapons, miniatures and snakes
te: The desert shrine of bronze weapons
se: At the foot of Jabal Mudhmar near Adam, a 2,800-year-old building held bronze bows, quivers, daggers and axes, some made too small to use
sa: عند سفح جبل مضمار قرب آدم، ضمّ مبنى عمره نحو 2800 عام أقواسًا وجعابًا وخناجر وفؤوسًا برونزية، صُنع بعضها أصغر من أن يُستعمل
desc: Mudhmar East lies at the eastern tip of Jabal Mudhmar near Wadi Dalfayn, about 45 km from Salut, and was discovered in 2009 by the French archaeological mission in central Oman led by Guillaume Gernez. The larger of two main buildings, about 15 m long and built of cut sandstone blocks and earth bricks, held five battle-axes, five daggers with crescent-shaped pommels, about fifty arrowheads, five complete bows averaging about 70 cm and two bronze quivers of about 35 cm, each with six arrows. Many weapons are full size, others are reduced models or miniatures, which suggests a ritual purpose; the second building held small bronze snakes and fragments of ceramic incense burners. The site dates to Iron Age II (900–600 BC) and may have been a meeting place with social, political or religious roles, or a staging post on the ancient road between Adam and Sinaw.
sig: The first non-utilitarian weapon deposit known from the Arabian Peninsula, linked to Iron Age rituals on the desert edge of central Oman.
refs: Gernez, G., Jean, M. & Benoist, A. (2017). The discovery of a new Iron Age ritual complex in central Oman: recent excavations near Ādam. Proceedings of the Seminar for Arabian Studies 47, 101–117. https://www.archaeopresspublishing.com/ojs/index.php/PSAS/article/view/1222

Kuronuma, T., Miki, T., Tanabe, K. & Kondo, Y. (2023). Iron Age landscape in the Tanuf District, Ad-Dākhliyyah Governorate. The Journal of Oman Studies 24, Table 1. https://archaeopresspublishing.com/ojs/index.php/jos/article/download/3206/2748/20223
CNRS (2016). First non-utilitarian weapons found in the Arabian Peninsula. ScienceDaily, 10 March 2016. https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/03/160310080816.htm
conf: Coordinates are the published point 22.459 N, 57.650 E for Madmar East (Kuronuma et al. 2023, Table 1), about 100 m precision. Spellings vary (Mudhmar, Madmar, Muḍmār); Arabic مضمار is a careful transliteration. Timeline from the 900–600 BC range

s: Mud-brick harat of a desert-edge oasis · birthplace of the founder of the Al Busaidi dynasty
dr: Old quarters, some reportedly pre-Islamic in origin
el: Harat al Busaid has about 120 old houses and six towers
te: The oasis at the desert’s door
se: At Adam, last oasis before the open desert, old mud-brick quarters with round towers once welcomed trading caravans
sa: في آدم، آخر واحة قبل الصحراء المفتوحة، احتضنت حارات قديمة من الطين ذات أبراج دائرية قوافل التجارة
desc: Adam is a fertile oasis wilayat in Ad Dakhiliyah, about 225 km from Muscat on the edge of the central desert, watered by aflaj and described as a former hub for trade caravans. Its old quarters include Harat bani Shaiban, with about 70 houses, three-storey circular towers and three mosques; Harat al Hawashim, circular in plan with two gates and two towers; and Harat al Busaid, one of the oldest, with about 120 houses and six defensive towers. The houses and mosques were built of clay, stone and plaster on stone foundations 1–2 m deep with juss mortar, and some quarters are reported to be pre-Islamic in origin. Harat al Busaid is described as the birthplace of Ahmad bin Said, founder of the Al Busaidi dynasty.
sig: A well-preserved example of the fortified mud-brick quarters of Oman’s interior oases, tied to the origins of the Al Busaidi state.
disc: About 120 houses in Harat al Busaid
refs: Oman Observer. Home to a vibrant history. https://www.omanobserver.om/article/26073/Local/home-to-a-vibrant-history
conf: Coordinates are the Wikipedia point for Adam town (22°23′N, 57°32′E), minute precision (≈1–2 km), not a point on a single quarter. Timeline is a broad estimate (no construction dates in the sources). About 14 km from Mudhmar East

s: Fog-fed limestone desert plateau of central Oman · Key Biodiversity Area of about 26,700 km²
se: On this vast stony plain, sea fog waters shrubs that feed gazelles, ibex, eagles and larks
sa: في هذا السهل الحجري الشاسع يسقي ضباب البحر الشجيرات التي تقتات عليها الغزلان والوعول والعقبان والقنابر
desc: Jiddat al-Harasis is a limestone plateau of sandy depressions, gravel plains, karst, dunes and escarpments covering about 26,742 km² of central Oman, recognised as a Key Biodiversity Area. Sea fog supports relatively good cover of low shrubs, ephemeral grasses and occasional acacias, and water seepages along the Al Huqf escarpment act as a refuge for animals. Recorded species include golden eagle, houbara bustard, crowned and spotted sandgrouse, Dunn’s lark, Arabian gazelle, Nubian ibex, Arabian wolf, caracal, reintroduced Arabian oryx and the endemic lizard Uromastyx thomasi, with several plants nearly restricted to the site. In 2015 Arabian gazelles on the surveyed plateau of the Al Wusta Wildlife Reserve numbered about 275, a density of 0.161 per km², well below earlier levels.
sig: The core desert habitat of central Oman’s gazelles, ibex and desert birds, much wider than the fenced oryx reserve inside it.
ex: KBA factsheet 8233; Al Jahdhami et al. (2017)
refs: KBA Partnership. Jiddat al Harasis (KBA 8233). Key Biodiversity Areas factsheet. https://www.keybiodiversityareas.org/site/factsheet/8233

Al Jahdhami, M.H. et al. (2017). The status of Arabian Gazelles Gazella arabica in Al Wusta Wildlife Reserve and Ras Ash Shajar Nature Reserve, Oman. Journal of Threatened Taxa 9(7), 10369–10373. https://doi.org/10.11609/jott.3398.9.7.10369-10373
conf: Coordinates are the published KBA centre point of a very large area (≈ tens of km); t0 counts from the 1994 assessment. About 66 km from the existing Al Wusta Wildlife Reserve point, which lies inside the plateau

s: Landlocked freshwater lagoon of the Sahil al Jazir · at least 121 bird species
te: A freshwater pool beside the sea
se: A small lagoon among the dunes of Al Wusta where ducks, terns and gulls rest and gazelles come to drink
sa: بحيرة صغيرة بين كثبان الوسطى تستريح فيها البط والخطاطيف البحرية والنوارس، وتقصدها الغزلان
desc: Khawr Dhirif is a landlocked, mostly freshwater lagoon of about 900 × 600 m on the Sahil al Jazir coastal plain of Al Wusta, recognised as a Key Biodiversity Area of about 0.98 km². It is surrounded by flat sandy terrain and dunes, with salt-tolerant shrubs near the water and aquatic Potamogeton and Ruppia. At least 121 bird species have been recorded, including wintering and migrating ducks such as ferruginous duck (Aythya nyroca), gulls, and gull-billed, Caspian, greater crested and Sandwich terns; Arabian gazelles are regularly seen. The lagoon lies within the proposed North Jazir National Nature Reserve of 15,000 ha.
sig: A rare freshwater stopover for waterbirds on the arid Al Wusta coast.
refs: KBA Partnership. Khor Dirif (KBA 8235). Key Biodiversity Areas factsheet. https://www.keybiodiversityareas.org/site/factsheet/8235
conf: Coordinates are the published KBA centre point (18.9333, 57.3500), about 1 km precision; t0 counts from the 1994 assessment. Arabic خور ذرف is a careful transliteration of the national name Khawr Dhirif. About 85 km from Khawr Ghawi
